claim: Feedforward inhibitory circuits are key contributors to the complex interplay between excitation and inhibition in the brain.
source: Feedforward inhibitory circuits are key contributors to the complex interplay between excitation and inhibition in the brain.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about feedforward inhibition.

claim: Odors evoke strong excitation in neurogliaform (NG) cells in layer 1 of the piriform cortex.
source: Using in vivo two-photon-targeted patch clamping and calcium imaging in mice, we find that odors evoke strong excitation in two classes of interneurons – neurogliaform (NG) cells and horizontal (HZ) cells – that provide feedforward inhibition in layer 1 of the piriform cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings shown in Figures 1E, 3, and 4.

claim: Odors evoke strong excitation in horizontal (HZ) cells in layer 1 of the piriform cortex.
source: Using in vivo two-photon-targeted patch clamping and calcium imaging in mice, we find that odors evoke strong excitation in two classes of interneurons – neurogliaform (NG) cells and horizontal (HZ) cells – that provide feedforward inhibition in layer 1 of the piriform cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings shown in Figures 1F, 3, and 4.

claim: NG cells and HZ cells provide feedforward inhibition in layer 1 of the piriform cortex.
source: Using in vivo two-photon-targeted patch clamping and calcium imaging in mice, we find that odors evoke strong excitation in two classes of interneurons – neurogliaform (NG) cells and horizontal (HZ) cells – that provide feedforward inhibition in layer 1 of the piriform cortex.
evidence: This is supported by the circuit architecture described in Figure 1A and previous literature cited in the introduction.

claim: NG cells fire much earlier than HZ cells following odor onset.
source: NG cells fire much earlier than HZ cells following odor onset, a difference that can be attributed to the faster odor-driven excitatory synaptic drive that NG cells receive from the olfactory bulb.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3A showing that spiking in NG cells reached a peak at 0.43 ± 0.14 s after odor onset (n = 7 cells), whereas in HZ cells the peak occurred at 1.92 ± 0.24 s (n = 5 cells; significantly different, p = 0.0013).

claim: The difference in firing timing between NG and HZ cells can be attributed to the faster odor-driven excitatory synaptic drive that NG cells receive from the olfactory bulb.
source: NG cells fire much earlier than HZ cells following odor onset, a difference that can be attributed to the faster odor-driven excitatory synaptic drive that NG cells receive from the olfactory bulb.
evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp data in Figure 5C showing that the time between odor onset and EPSC peak was about twofold faster in NG cells than in HZ cells (NG: 0.72 ± 0.09 s, n = 30 cell-odor pairs; HZ: 1.24 ± 0.12 s, n = 21 cell-odor pairs; p = 0.0014).

claim: NG cells strongly but transiently inhibit odor-evoked excitation in layer 2 principal cells.
source: As a result, NG cells strongly but transiently inhibit odor-evoked excitation in layer 2 principal cells, whereas HZ cells provide more diffuse and prolonged feedforward inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by slice simulation data in Figure 7B showing that NG cells significantly suppress early firing in SP cells (p < 0.001, KS test).

claim: HZ cells provide more diffuse and prolonged feedforward inhibition to layer 2 principal cells.
source: As a result, NG cells strongly but transiently inhibit odor-evoked excitation in layer 2 principal cells, whereas HZ cells provide more diffuse and prolonged feedforward inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7A and 7B showing that HZ cells generate a smaller and more diffuse IPSP that persists beyond the end of odor application.

claim: Cortical interneurons are classified into dozens of subtypes with distinctive morphological, transcriptomic, and electrophysiological properties.
source: Cortical interneurons are classified into dozens of subtypes with distinctive morphological, transcriptomic, and electrophysiological properties (Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1997; Tremblay et al., 2016; Zeng, 2017; Gouwens et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cortical interneurons are embedded in at least three types of cortical inhibitory circuits: feedforward inhibition, feedback inhibition, and disinhibition.
source: These diverse interneurons are embedded in at least three types of cortical inhibitory circuits – feedforward inhibition, feedback inhibition, and disinhibition (Kullmann and Lamsa, 2007; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Denève and Machens, 2016; Tremblay et al., 2016; Lourenço et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Feedforward inhibition is conventionally understood as an input-tracking mechanism that does not depend on local circuit activity.
source: Feedforward inhibition is conventionally understood as an input-tracking mechanism that does not depend on local circuit activity (Tremblay et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the primary neocortex, feedforward inhibition is often mediated by parvalbumin-expressing fast-spiking basket cells localized in the deeper layers that receive direct afferent input from first-order thalamic nuclei.
source: In the primary neocortex, feedforward inhibition is often mediated by parvalbumin-expressing fast-spiking basket cells localized in the deeper layers that receive direct afferent input from first-order thalamic nuclei (Beierlein et al., 2003; Gabernet et al., 2005; Cruikshank et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Feedforward inhibition improves sensory discrimination by favoring coincidence detection.
source: In this role feedforward inhibition improves sensory discrimination by favoring coincidence detection, but in addition it can provide gain modulation through input normalization (Bruno and Sakmann, 2006; Carandini and Heeger, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Feedforward inhibition can provide gain modulation through input normalization.
source: In this role feedforward inhibition improves sensory discrimination by favoring coincidence detection, but in addition it can provide gain modulation through input normalization (Bruno and Sakmann, 2006; Carandini and Heeger, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Feedforward inhibition is also prominent in layer 1 of the neocortex, where it can engage afferent input from other cortical regions and from higher-order thalamic nuclei.
source: More recently it has been reported that feedforward inhibition is also prominent in layer 1 of the neocortex, where it can engage afferent input from other cortical regions and from higher-order thalamic nuclei (Pardi et al., 2020; Anastasiades et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The piriform cortex receives all of its primary afferent input from the olfactory bulb into the superficial part of layer 1 (layer 1a).
source: The piriform cortex (PCx) is unusual in that it receives all of its primary afferent input from the olfactory bulb into the superficial part of layer 1 (layer 1a; Neville and Haberly, 2004; Bekkers and Suzuki, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Layer 1a of the piriform cortex mostly contains the apical dendrites of glutamatergic principal cells located in layers 2 and 3.
source: Layer 1a mostly contains the apical dendrites of glutamatergic principal cells located in layers 2 and 3, as well as the somas, axons, and dendrites of two classes of GABAergic interneurons, namely, neurogliaform (NG) cells and horizontal (HZ) cells (Suzuki and Bekkers, 2010a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Layer 1a of the piriform cortex contains the somas, axons, and dendrites of two classes of GABAergic interneurons: neurogliaform (NG) cells and horizontal (HZ) cells.
source: Layer 1a mostly contains the apical dendrites of glutamatergic principal cells located in layers 2 and 3, as well as the somas, axons, and dendrites of two classes of GABAergic interneurons, namely, neurogliaform (NG) cells and horizontal (HZ) cells (Suzuki and Bekkers, 2010a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: NG and HZ cells in layer 1a are ideally situated to provide feedforward inhibition onto the distal dendrites of layer 2/3 principal cells.
source: NG and HZ cells in layer 1a are thus ideally situated to provide feedforward inhibition onto the distal dendrites of layer 2/3 principal cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical location of these cells as described in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The existence and importance of odor-evoked inhibition in the piriform cortex has been established.
source: The existence and importance of odor-evoked inhibition in the PCx has been established (Poo and Isaacson, 2009; Zhan and Luo, 2010; Franks et al., 2011; Poo and Isaacson, 2011; Sturgill and Isaacson, 2015; Bolding and Franks, 2017; Tantirigama et al., 2017; Bolding and Franks, 2018) but the identities and properties of neurons responsible for the different kinds of inhibition are, for the most part, uncertain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The identities and properties of neurons responsible for the different kinds of inhibition in the piriform cortex are, for the most part, uncertain.
source: The existence and importance of odor-evoked inhibition in the PCx has been established (Poo and Isaacson, 2009; Zhan and Luo, 2010; Franks et al., 2011; Poo and Isaacson, 2011; Sturgill and Isaacson, 2015; Bolding and Franks, 2017; Tantirigama et al., 2017; Bolding and Franks, 2018) but the identities and properties of neurons responsible for the different kinds of inhibition are, for the most part, uncertain.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field based on the cited literature.

claim: In GAD67-GFP (Δneo) mice, HZ cells are only found close to the LOT whereas NG cells are distributed throughout L1a.
source: In GAD67-GFP (Δneo) mice, NG and HZ cells can readily be distinguished under the two-photon microscope: HZ cells are only found close to the LOT whereas NG cells are distributed throughout L1a; HZ cell somata have an elongated shape whereas NG somata are spherical; and HZ cells express much lower levels of GFP than NG cells (Figure 1B, top; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2010a; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2010b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: HZ cell somata have an elongated shape whereas NG somata are spherical.
source: In GAD67-GFP (Δneo) mice, NG and HZ cells can readily be distinguished under the two-photon microscope: HZ cells are only found close to the LOT whereas NG cells are distributed throughout L1a; HZ cell somata have an elongated shape whereas NG somata are spherical; and HZ cells express much lower levels of GFP than NG cells (Figure 1B, top; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2010a; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2010b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: HZ cells express much lower levels of GFP than NG cells in GAD67-GFP (Δneo) mice.
source: In GAD67-GFP (Δneo) mice, NG and HZ cells can readily be distinguished under the two-photon microscope: HZ cells are only found close to the LOT whereas NG cells are distributed throughout L1a; HZ cell somata have an elongated shape whereas NG somata are spherical; and HZ cells express much lower levels of GFP than NG cells (Figure 1B, top; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2010a; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2010b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and is illustrated in Figure 1B showing the difference in GFP fluorescence.

claim: NG cells have short, thin, highly branched dendrites.
source: After whole-cell recording, their identities could be confirmed by their dendritic morphology (NG: short, thin, highly branched dendrites; HZ: longer, less branched, often spiny; Figure 1B, bottom) and distinctive intrinsic electrical properties (Figure 1C and D), similar to in vitro (Suzuki and Bekkers, 2010a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and is illustrated in Figure 1B bottom.

claim: HZ cells have longer, less branched, often spiny dendrites.
source: After whole-cell recording, their identities could be confirmed by their dendritic morphology (NG: short, thin, highly branched dendrites; HZ: longer, less branched, often spiny; Figure 1B, bottom) and distinctive intrinsic electrical properties (Figure 1C and D), similar to in vitro (Suzuki and Bekkers, 2010a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and is illustrated in Figure 1B bottom.

claim: NG and HZ cells have distinctive intrinsic electrical properties similar to in vitro.
source: After whole-cell recording, their identities could be confirmed by their dendritic morphology (NG: short, thin, highly branched dendrites; HZ: longer, less branched, often spiny; Figure 1B, bottom) and distinctive intrinsic electrical properties (Figure 1C and D), similar to in vitro (Suzuki and Bekkers, 2010a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and is illustrated in Figure 1C and D showing differences in action potential properties.

claim: Both NG and HZ cells respond to many different odors (i.e. they are broadly tuned).
source: Three features were apparent in these responses: first, both cell types responded to many different odors (i.e. they were broadly tuned); second, regular oscillations in the membrane potential (Vm) often became larger in the presence of odor; and third, HZ cells appeared to respond more slowly to odors than did NG cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1E and F showing responses to multiple odors, and quantified in the Results section.

claim: Regular oscillations in the membrane potential (Vm) often became larger in the presence of odor in NG and HZ cells.
source: Three features were apparent in these responses: first, both cell types responded to many different odors (i.e. they were broadly tuned); second, regular oscillations in the membrane potential (Vm) often became larger in the presence of odor; and third, HZ cells appeared to respond more slowly to odors than did NG cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2 showing increased oscillation amplitude during odor application.

claim: HZ cells appeared to respond more slowly to odors than did NG cells.
source: Three features were apparent in these responses: first, both cell types responded to many different odors (i.e. they were broadly tuned); second, regular oscillations in the membrane potential (Vm) often became larger in the presence of odor; and third, HZ cells appeared to respond more slowly to odors than did NG cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3 showing delayed firing in HZ cells compared to NG cells.

claim: The cell-averaged odor responsiveness index for NG cells is 0.78 ± 0.04 (n = 28 cells from 19 mice).
source: NG and HZ cells both had large cell-averaged indices that were not significantly different from each other (NG: 0.78 ± 0.04, n = 28 cells from 19 mice; HZ: 0.66 ± 0.12, n = 9 cells from 9 mice; p = 0.34, Welch's two-sample unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis described in the Results section.

claim: The cell-averaged odor responsiveness index for HZ cells is 0.66 ± 0.12 (n = 9 cells from 9 mice).
source: NG and HZ cells both had large cell-averaged indices that were not significantly different from each other (NG: 0.78 ± 0.04, n = 28 cells from 19 mice; HZ: 0.66 ± 0.12, n = 9 cells from 9 mice; p = 0.34, Welch's two-sample unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis described in the Results section.

claim: The cell-averaged odor responsiveness indices for NG and HZ cells are not significantly different from each other (p = 0.34).
source: NG and HZ cells both had large cell-averaged indices that were not significantly different from each other (NG: 0.78 ± 0.04, n = 28 cells from 19 mice; HZ: 0.66 ± 0.12, n = 9 cells from 9 mice; p = 0.34, Welch's two-sample unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: The odor-averaged index for NG cells is 0.75 ± 0.03 (n = 15 odors).
source: The odor-averaged index was also large for both cell types but was significantly smaller for HZ cells (NG: 0.75 ± 0.03, n = 15 odors; HZ: 0.60 ± 0.06, n = 15; p = 0.025, Welch's two-sample unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis described in the Results section.

claim: The odor-averaged index for HZ cells is 0.60 ± 0.06 (n = 15 odors).
source: The odor-averaged index was also large for both cell types but was significantly smaller for HZ cells (NG: 0.75 ± 0.03, n = 15 odors; HZ: 0.60 ± 0.06, n = 15; p = 0.025, Welch's two-sample unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis described in the Results section.

claim: The odor-averaged index is significantly smaller for HZ cells compared to NG cells (p = 0.025).
source: The odor-averaged index was also large for both cell types but was significantly smaller for HZ cells (NG: 0.75 ± 0.03, n = 15 odors; HZ: 0.60 ± 0.06, n = 15; p = 0.025, Welch's two-sample unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Subthreshold oscillations in Vm were frequently seen in both NG and HZ cells.
source: Subthreshold oscillations in Vm were frequently seen in both NG and HZ cells (e.g. Figure 2A and B, top, show the same cells as in Figure 1E and F responding to ethyl-n-butyrate; gray traces are respiration, with upward transients indicating onset of exhalation).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Oscillations in Vm were synchronized to respiration in NG and HZ cells.
source: Expanding the traces in windows before (b), during (d), and after (a) odor application revealed that oscillations in Vm were synchronized to respiration and, at least in the NG cell, the amplitude of Vm oscillations appeared to increase during the odor (Figure 2A and B, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B bottom panels.

claim: The peak-to-peak Vm amplitude increased significantly during odor application in NG cells (b: 7.7 ± 0.8 mV; d: 11.1 ± 1.2 mV; n = 12, p = 0.002).
source: For this particular NG cell, the peak-to-peak Vm amplitude increased significantly during the odor (b: 7.7 ± 0.8 mV; d: 11.1 ± 1.2 mV; n = 12, p = 0.002, one-way ANOVA with Tukey's contrasts), whereas the phase of the peak was unchanged (b: 0.49 ± 0.02; d: 0.45 ± 0.03, both expressed as a fraction of the respiration cycle; p = 0.47).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis of the NG cell shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The phase of the peak Vm was unchanged during odor application in NG cells (b: 0.49 ± 0.02; d: 0.45 ± 0.03; p = 0.47).
source: For this particular NG cell, the peak-to-peak Vm amplitude increased significantly during the odor (b: 7.7 ± 0.8 mV; d: 11.1 ± 1.2 mV; n = 12, p = 0.002, one-way ANOVA with Tukey's contrasts), whereas the phase of the peak was unchanged (b: 0.49 ± 0.02; d: 0.45 ± 0.03, both expressed as a fraction of the respiration cycle; p = 0.47).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis of the NG cell shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The mean peak-to-peak Vm amplitude increased significantly during odors in NG cells (n = 232 trials in 22 NG cells, p < 0.0002).
source: The mean peak-to-peak Vm amplitude increased significantly during odors in NG cells but not in HZ cells (Figure 2D, left; n = 232 trials in 22 NG cells, p < 0.0002; n = 98 trials in 9 HZ cells, p = 0.78; one-way ANOVA with Tukey).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The mean peak-to-peak Vm amplitude did not increase significantly during odors in HZ cells (n = 98 trials in 9 HZ cells, p = 0.78).
source: The mean peak-to-peak Vm amplitude increased significantly during odors in NG cells but not in HZ cells (Figure 2D, left; n = 232 trials in 22 NG cells, p < 0.0002; n = 98 trials in 9 HZ cells, p = 0.78; one-way ANOVA with Tukey).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The phase of the peak Vm was unchanged by odors in both NG and HZ cells.
source: In contrast, the phase of the peak Vm was unchanged by odors in both NG and HZ cells (Figure 2D, right).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis shown in Figure 2D right panel.

claim: Spiking in NG cells reached a peak at 0.43 ± 0.14 s after odor onset (n = 7 cells).
source: We confirmed this impression by constructing AP raster plots and peristimulus time histograms (Figure 3A): spiking in NG cells reached a peak at 0.43 ± 0.14 s after odor onset (n = 7 cells), whereas in HZ cells the peak occurred at 1.92 ± 0.24 s (n = 5 cells; significantly different, p = 0.0013, Welch's two-sample unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Spiking in HZ cells reached a peak at 1.92 ± 0.24 s after odor onset (n = 5 cells).
source: We confirmed this impression by constructing AP raster plots and peristimulus time histograms (Figure 3A): spiking in NG cells reached a peak at 0.43 ± 0.14 s after odor onset (n = 7 cells), whereas in HZ cells the peak occurred at 1.92 ± 0.24 s (n = 5 cells; significantly different, p = 0.0013, Welch's two-sample unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The time to peak spiking after odor onset is significantly different between NG and HZ cells (p = 0.0013).
source: We confirmed this impression by constructing AP raster plots and peristimulus time histograms (Figure 3A): spiking in NG cells reached a peak at 0.43 ± 0.14 s after odor onset (n = 7 cells), whereas in HZ cells the peak occurred at 1.92 ± 0.24 s (n = 5 cells; significantly different, p = 0.0013, Welch's two-sample unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Ca2+ imaging showed that NG cells fired quickly after odor onset and HZ cells fired with a delay.
source: Consistent with whole-cell patch clamping (Figure 3A), Ca2+ imaging showed that NG cells fired quickly after odor onset and HZ cells fired with a delay (Figure 3B; traces are averages of n = 6 NG cells and n = 5 HZ cells; individual traces were too noisy to reliably determine the average time to peak).
evidence: This is a result from Ca2+ imaging experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The different odor-response dynamics of NG and HZ cells are not related to anesthesia.
source: These findings, together with a report that urethane at the relatively low concentration we used here has little effect on ligand-gated synaptic receptors (Hara and Harris, 2002), suggest that the different odor-response dynamics of NG and HZ cells are not related to anesthesia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency of results across different anesthetics (urethane and fentanyl/medetomidine) and a citation about urethane's effects.

claim: Odor-evoked EPSPs reached their peak about twofold faster in NG cells than in HZ cells (NG: 0.53 ± 0.05 s, n = 16 cells; HZ: 1.26 ± 0.26 s, n = 6 cells; p = 0.038).
source: The analysis showed that odor-evoked EPSPs reached their peak about twofold faster in NG cells than in HZ cells (Figure 4A; NG: 0.53 ± 0.05 s, n = 16 cells; HZ: 1.26 ± 0.26 s, n = 6 cells; p = 0.038, Welch's two-sample unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The slower-rising EPSPs in HZ cells can explain the longer delay to firing of these cells.
source: Thus, the slower-rising EPSPs in HZ cells (Figure 4A) can explain the longer delay to firing of these cells (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the EPSP kinetics data to the firing delay data.

claim: During odors, EPSPs in NG cells tend to decline from an early peak while EPSPs in HZ cells tend to rise to a later peak.
source: Thus, during odors, EPSPs in NG cells tend to decline from an early peak while EPSPs in HZ cells tend to rise to a later peak.
evidence: This is a summary of the data analysis shown in Figure 4C showing different EPSP slope distributions for NG and HZ cells.

claim: The EPSP slopes for NG and HZ cells during odor application were significantly different (NG slope: –0.27 ± 0.02, n = 232 trials; HZ slope: 0.21 ± 0.04, n = 84 trials; p < 0.001, KS test).
source: Histograms of all the remaining trials confirm that the EPSP slopes for NG and HZ cells were significantly different (Figure 4C, bottom; NG slope, –0.27 ± 0.02, n = 232 trials above the z-score threshold; HZ slope, 0.21 ± 0.04, n = 84 trials above threshold; p < 0.001, Kolmogorov-Smirnov [KS] test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: For brief trains of stimuli (6 pulses at 40 Hz), NG cells facilitated and HZ cells depressed, which is the opposite of what was required to explain the in vivo odor responses.
source: For brief trains of stimuli (6 pulses at 40 Hz, modeled on in vivo patterns; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2006), the response was the exact opposite of what was required: NG cells facilitated and HZ cells depressed (Figure 5B, top).
evidence: This is a result from slice experiments shown in Figure 5B top.

claim: A train of 40 Hz stimuli repeating at 3 Hz produced a modestly depressing envelope of EPSPs in both NG and HZ cells.
source: We next tried a more realistic model of odor-evoked afferent excitation, that is, a train of 40 Hz stimuli repeating at 3 Hz (the approximate respiration frequency in mice; Poo and Isaacson, 2009). This stimulus produced a modestly depressing envelope of EPSPs in both NG and HZ cells (Figure 5B, bottom).
evidence: This is a result from slice experiments shown in Figure 5B bottom.

claim: The short-term dynamics of the LOT afferents could explain the declining response during odors in NG cells but not the facilitating response in HZ cells.
source: Thus, the short-term dynamics of the LOT afferents could explain the declining response during odors in NG cells but not the facilitating response in HZ cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the slice experiment results in Figure 5B.

claim: The time between odor onset and EPSC peak was about twofold faster in NG cells than in HZ cells (NG: 0.72 ± 0.09 s, n = 30 cell-odor pairs; HZ: 1.24 ± 0.12 s, n = 21 cell-odor pairs; p = 0.0014).
source: Similar to the result for EPSPs (previous section), the time between odor onset and EPSC peak was about twofold faster in NG cells than in HZ cells (NG: 0.72 ± 0.09 s, n = 30 cell-odor pairs; HZ: 1.24 ± 0.12 s, n = 21 cell-odor pairs; p = 0.0014, Welch's two-sample unpaired t-test; Figure 5C inset, bottom).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from voltage clamp experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The slower EPSC rise time in HZ cells is consistent with the slower-rising EPSP and the delayed onset of odor-evoked spiking in HZ cells.
source: Thus, given that the membrane time constant is fast (~4 ms) and not significantly different between NG and HZ cells (Suzuki and Bekkers, 2010a), the slower EPSC rise time in HZ cells is consistent with the slower-rising EPSP (Figure 4A) and the delayed onset of odor-evoked spiking (Figure 3) in HZ cells.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the EPSC kinetics data to the EPSP and spiking data, with a citation about membrane time constants.

claim: The dynamics of excitatory synaptic inputs at least partially determine the delayed odor responses of HZ cells.
source: In summary, despite the in vitro finding that HZ cells do not receive facilitating EPSPs from the LOT (Figure 5B), both current clamp (Figure 4A) and voltage clamp (Figure 5C) experiments in vivo show that HZ cells receive slower-rising synaptic inputs than NG cells. Thus, the dynamics of excitatory synaptic inputs at least partially determine the delayed odor responses of HZ cells, although the origin of these slower dynamics remains unclear (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: Odor-evoked IPSCs were present in both HZ and NG cells.
source: We addressed this possibility by making in vivo whole-cell voltage clamp recordings to look for odor-evoked IPSCs in isolation at a holding potential of +10 mV (Poo and Isaacson, 2009). Such IPSCs were, indeed, present in both HZ and NG cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a result from voltage clamp experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The properties of odor-evoked IPSCs were not significantly different between NG and HZ cells (mean amplitude: 50.3 ± 4.3 pA versus 49.9 ± 11.0 pA; time to peak: 0.58 ± 0.12 s versus 0.35 ± 0.05 s; all p > 0.1).
source: Their properties were not significantly different between the two cell types (mean amplitude: 50.3 ± 4.3 pA versus 49.9 ± 11.0 pA; time to peak: 0.58 ± 0.12 s versus 0.35 ± 0.05 s; data for NG and HZ cells, respectively; all p > 0.1, n = 14 and 5 cell-odor pairs, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis of IPSCs.

claim: NG→HZ cell connections were frequent and strong (14/43 = 32.6% connectivity; mean connection conductance 0.87 ± 0.41 nS, range 0.10–5.86 nS, n = 14 pairs).
source: These experiments revealed that NG→HZ cell connections were frequent and strong (Figure 6B; 14/43 = 32.6% connectivity; mean connection conductance 0.87 ± 0.41 nS, range 0.10–5.86 nS, n = 14 pairs) whereas the reverse connection was never seen (0/13 = 0%; significantly different, p = 0.02, chi-square 2 × 2 contingency test).
evidence: This is a result from paired recordings in slices shown in Figure 6B.

claim: HZ→NG cell connections were never observed (0/13 = 0%).
source: These experiments revealed that NG→HZ cell connections were frequent and strong (Figure 6B; 14/43 = 32.6% connectivity; mean connection conductance 0.87 ± 0.41 nS, range 0.10–5.86 nS, n = 14 pairs) whereas the reverse connection was never seen (0/13 = 0%; significantly different, p = 0.02, chi-square 2 × 2 contingency test).
evidence: This is a result from paired recordings in slices shown in Figure 6B.

claim: NG→HZ connectivity is significantly different from HZ→NG connectivity (p = 0.02).
source: These experiments revealed that NG→HZ cell connections were frequent and strong (Figure 6B; 14/43 = 32.6% connectivity; mean connection conductance 0.87 ± 0.41 nS, range 0.10–5.86 nS, n = 14 pairs) whereas the reverse connection was never seen (0/13 = 0%; significantly different, p = 0.02, chi-square 2 × 2 contingency test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the paired recording experiments.

claim: NG→NG cell connectivity is 2/17 = 11.8%.
source: NG→NG cell connectivity (2/17 = 11.8%) was not significantly different from NG→HZ connectivity (p = 0.1, chi-square 2 × 2 contingency test; Figure 6B, right) although the n-values are modest.
evidence: This is a result from paired recordings in slices shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Connectivity between HZ cells was weaker (1/19 = 5.3%).
source: In contrast, connectivity between HZ cells was weaker (1/19 = 5.3%; Figure 6B, right).
evidence: This is a result from paired recordings in slices shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Odor-evoked synaptic inhibition of both NG and HZ cells most likely comes from NG cells after they are excited by the LOT.
source: To sum up, these connectivity experiments suggest that odor-evoked synaptic inhibition of both NG and HZ cells most likely comes from NG cells after they are excited by the LOT.
evidence: This is an inference based on the connectivity data in Figure 6B.

claim: The EPSC in the NG cell was always much smaller than that in the HZ cell for the first EPSC in a train of LOT stimuli.
source: Notably, the EPSC in the NG cell was always much smaller than that in the HZ cell for the first EPSC in the train (e.g. Figure 6C, bottom left and top right).
evidence: This is a result from dual recordings in slices shown in Figure 6C.

claim: For the first EPSC in a train, the mean NG:HZ amplitude ratio was 0.27 ± 0.03 (n = 7 cell pairs).
source: For the first EPSC, the mean NG:HZ amplitude ratio was 0.27 ± 0.03 (mean ± standard error of the mean [SEM], n = 7 cell pairs), but by the third EPSC this ratio had increased to 1.38 ± 0.32 (significantly different, p = 0.0002, n = 7, one-way ANOVA with Tukey; Figure 6C, bottom right).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from dual recordings shown in Figure 6C.

claim: By the third EPSC in a train, the NG:HZ amplitude ratio had increased to 1.38 ± 0.32 (significantly different from the first EPSC, p = 0.0002).
source: For the first EPSC, the mean NG:HZ amplitude ratio was 0.27 ± 0.03 (mean ± standard error of the mean [SEM], n = 7 cell pairs), but by the third EPSC this ratio had increased to 1.38 ± 0.32 (significantly different, p = 0.0002, n = 7, one-way ANOVA with Tukey; Figure 6C, bottom right).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from dual recordings shown in Figure 6C.

claim: NG cells do not receive privileged input from the LOT compared to HZ cells; rather, the reverse is the case for the first EPSC in a train.
source: These results show that NG cells do not receive privileged input from the LOT compared to HZ cells; rather, the reverse is the case for the first EPSC in a train.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dual recording data in Figure 6C.

claim: NG and HZ cells mostly operate in a regime where they receive similar afferent excitation.
source: Given the known dynamics of afferent input from the olfactory bulb (i.e. modulated bursts of APs; Cang and Isaacson, 2003; Margrie and Schaefer, 2003), these results suggest that NG and HZ cells mostly operate in a regime where they receive similar afferent excitation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dual recording data and citations about olfactory bulb dynamics.

claim: NG cells generate a large, rapid IPSP in SP cells.
source: These results show that NG cells generate a large, rapid IPSP in SP cells, whereas HZ cells generate a smaller and more diffuse IPSP that persists beyond the end of odor application.
evidence: This is a result from slice experiments shown in Figure 7A.

claim: HZ cells generate a smaller and more diffuse IPSP in SP cells that persists beyond the end of odor application.
source: These results show that NG cells generate a large, rapid IPSP in SP cells, whereas HZ cells generate a smaller and more diffuse IPSP that persists beyond the end of odor application.
evidence: This is a result from slice experiments shown in Figure 7A.

claim: NG cells strongly suppress early odor-evoked firing in SP cells (p < 0.001, KS test).
source: The results confirm that NG cells strongly suppress early odor-evoked firing in SP cells (p < 0.001, KS test), whereas HZ cells tend to have a weaker, delayed effect (here, not significant; p = 0.81, KS test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from slice experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: HZ cells tend to have a weaker, delayed effect on odor-evoked firing in SP cells (not significant; p = 0.81, KS test).
source: The results confirm that NG cells strongly suppress early odor-evoked firing in SP cells (p < 0.001, KS test), whereas HZ cells tend to have a weaker, delayed effect (here, not significant; p = 0.81, KS test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from slice experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Urethane at the relatively low concentration used in this study (0.7 g/kg) has little effect on ligand-gated synaptic receptors.
source: These findings, together with a report that urethane at the relatively low concentration we used here has little effect on ligand-gated synaptic receptors (Hara and Harris, 2002), suggest that the different odor-response dynamics of NG and HZ cells are not related to anesthesia.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Urethane at 0.7 g/kg has no effect on electrical activity in the PCx compared with mice anesthetized with fentanyl/medetomidine.
source: Urethane has been widely used in previous in vivo studies of the PCx (e.g. Barnes et al., 2008; Poo and Isaacson, 2009; Poo and Isaacson, 2011; Wesson et al., 2011; Chapuis and Wilson, 2011; Sturgill and Isaacson, 2015), and we have confirmed that urethane at this concentration has no effect on electrical activity in the PCx compared with mice anesthetized with fentanyl/medetomidine (which induces a more awake-like brain state; Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Constantinople and Bruno, 2011; Tantirigama et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and citations to previous literature.

claim: Broad tuning of odor-evoked EPSPs in NG and HZ cells is consistent with previous findings.
source: We found broad tuning of odor-evoked EPSPs in NG and HZ cells, consistent with previous findings (Poo and Isaacson, 2009; odor-averaged index, 0.50 ± 0.04 cf 0.75 and 0.60 for NG and HZ cells, respectively, found here).
evidence: This claim compares the current findings to previous literature.

claim: Layer 1 interneurons receive a higher convergence of afferent input from the olfactory bulb than do principal neurons.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that layer 1 interneurons receive a higher convergence of afferent input from the olfactory bulb than do principal neurons (Poo and Isaacson, 2009; Miyamichi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Respiratory oscillations in Vm are ubiquitous in the olfactory system.
source: We often observed oscillations in subthreshold Vm that were phase-locked to respiration, consistent with previous reports that such oscillations are ubiquitous in the olfactory system (Fontanini and Bower, 2006; Kay et al., 2009; Poo and Isaacson, 2009; Wilson, 2010; Oswald and Urban, 2012; Kay, 2014; Jiang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Odor-dependent oscillations in Vm were functionally relevant because they generated respiratory-patterned IPSPs in target neurons.
source: These odor-dependent oscillations were functionally relevant because they generated respiratory-patterned IPSPs in target neurons (Figure 7A) and provided rhythmic inhibition of similarly patterned EPSPs (Figure 7B; see also Poo and Isaacson, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: NG cells provide fast, phase-critical feedforward inhibition whereas HZ cells provide a slower, tonic form of inhibition.
source: This difference between NG and HZ cells suggests that NG cells provide fast, phase-critical feedforward inhibition whereas HZ cells provide a slower, tonic form of inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differences in odor-dependent oscillations and inhibitory effects observed in the data.

claim: Mitral cells respond about twofold more slowly to odor stimulation than tufted cells.
source: Mitral cells have been reported to respond about twofold more slowly to odor stimulation than tufted cells (Fukunaga et al., 2012; Igarashi et al., 2012) because of differences in synaptic inhibition in the bulb (Fukunaga et al., 2012; Geramita and Urban, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The axons of tufted cells in the dorsal olfactory bulb do not extend far from the LOT and only reach about halfway along the length of the anterior PCx, that is, to ~1 mm anterior to Bregma.
source: A difficulty with this idea is that the axons of tufted cells in the dorsal olfactory bulb do not extend far from the LOT and only reach about halfway along the length of the anterior PCx, that is, to ~1 mm anterior to Bregma (Paxinos and Franklin, 2001; Igarashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: AON axons are sparser in layer 1a than in deeper layers, but they are consistently seen there.
source: Although AON axons are sparser in layer 1a than in deeper layers, they are consistently seen there (Haberly and Price, 1978; Hagiwara et al., 2012; Russo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Feedforward inhibition is generally recognized as an input-tracking mechanism which, in the hippocampus and neocortex, can synchronize spike timing.
source: Feedforward inhibition is generally recognized as an input-tracking mechanism which, in the hippocampus and neocortex, can synchronize spike timing (Pouille and Scanziani, 2001; Gabernet et al., 2005) and modulate gain through input normalization (Pouille et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Feedforward inhibition in the hippocampus and neocortex can modulate gain through input normalization.
source: Feedforward inhibition is generally recognized as an input-tracking mechanism which, in the hippocampus and neocortex, can synchronize spike timing (Pouille and Scanziani, 2001; Gabernet et al., 2005) and modulate gain through input normalization (Pouille et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The PCx is unusual in that it receives its feedforward inhibitory input onto the distal apical dendrites of principal cells, rather than onto perisomatic regions as in other cortices.
source: The PCx is unusual in that it receives its feedforward inhibitory input onto the distal apical dendrites of principal cells, rather than onto perisomatic regions as in other cortices (Lourenço et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and the anatomical data in this study.

claim: Feedforward inhibition works together with feedback inhibition to provide spatially and temporally modulated inhibition during bursts of olfactory input.
source: One slice study has shown that feedforward inhibition works together with feedback inhibition to provide spatially and temporally modulated inhibition during bursts of olfactory input (Stokes and Isaacson, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The shift in inhibition in the PCx is in the opposite direction to that found in other brain regions.
source: Intriguingly, the shift in inhibition reported by Stokes and Isaacson, 2010, is in the opposite direction to that found in other brain regions (Pouille and Scanziani, 2004; Silberberg and Markram, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Odor-evoked spiking in feedforward inhibitory neurons in the PCx increases only slowly and weakly after inhalation in awake mice.
source: More recently, an in vivo unit recording study in awake mice showed that odor-evoked spiking in feedforward inhibitory neurons in the PCx increases only slowly and weakly after inhalation, suggesting that these neurons provide tonic inhibition and do not play a major role in sculpting odor-evoked responses (Bolding and Franks, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Feedforward inhibition provides modest subtractive normalization in the PCx, in contrast to the divisive normalization it provides in other cortical regions.
source: Modeling confirmed that feedforward inhibition provides modest subtractive normalization in the PCx, in contrast to the divisive normalization it provides in other cortical regions (Stern et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PCx uses a temporal or rate-based code that is more susceptible to 'recurrent normalization' provided by feedback inhibition.
source: An intuitive explanation is that PCx uses a temporal or rate-based code that is more susceptible to 'recurrent normalization' provided by feedback inhibition (Sturgill and Isaacson, 2015; Bolding and Franks, 2018; Stern et al., 2018; Bolding et al., 2020; Pashkovski et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: By inhibiting the distal apical dendrites of layer 2/3 principal cells, NG and HZ cells have the potential to dampen passive propagation of afferent EPSPs to the soma and to veto dendritic electrogenesis.
source: By inhibiting the distal apical dendrites of layer 2/3 principal cells, NG and HZ cells have the potential to dampen passive propagation of afferent EPSPs to the soma and to veto dendritic electrogenesis (Larkum et al., 1999; Palmer et al., 2014; Pardi et al., 2020; Anastasiades et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical location of these cells and citations to previous literature about dendritic inhibition.

claim: A single layer 1 interneuron can inhibit Ca2+ signaling in the distal dendrites of PCx principal cells in a branch-specific fashion.
source: Indeed, it has been directly shown in vitro that a single layer 1 interneuron can inhibit Ca2+ signaling in the distal dendrites of PCx principal cells in a branch-specific fashion (Stokes et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Layer 1a NG cells generate slow-rising (2–3 ms) feedforward unitary IPSPs in layer 2 principal neurons.
source: We have previously shown in slices that layer 1a NG cells and HZ cells generate slow-rising (2–3 ms) and fast-rising (1 ms) feedforward unitary IPSPs, respectively, in layer 2 principal neurons, leading us to suggest that NG cell-mediated feedforward inhibition is slower and more diffuse than that provided by HZ cells (Suzuki and Bekkers, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: HZ cells generate fast-rising (1 ms) feedforward unitary IPSPs in layer 2 principal neurons.
source: We have previously shown in slices that layer 1a NG cells and HZ cells generate slow-rising (2–3 ms) and fast-rising (1 ms) feedforward unitary IPSPs, respectively, in layer 2 principal neurons, leading us to suggest that NG cell-mediated feedforward inhibition is slower and more diffuse than that provided by HZ cells (Suzuki and Bekkers, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: NG cells generate GABA transients that spill out of the synaptic cleft and can activate heterosynaptic GABAA and GABAB receptors.
source: For instance, NG cells generate GABA transients that spill out of the synaptic cleft and can activate heterosynaptic GABAA and GABAB receptors (Karayannis et al., 2010; Overstreet-Wadiche and McBain, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Trained rodents can discriminate odors within a single sniff (<100 ms).
source: Trained rodents can discriminate odors within a single sniff (<100 ms; Uchida and Mainen, 2003; Abraham et al., 2004; Rinberg et al., 2006; Resulaj and Rinberg, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HZ cells are only found close to the LOT (<~200 µm), giving them privileged inhibitory influence over a spatially restricted subset of principal cells.
source: First, HZ cells are only found close to the LOT (<~200 µm), giving them privileged inhibitory influence over a spatially restricted subset of principal cells (Suzuki and Bekkers, 2010a; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HZ cells are the only class of interneuron in the PCx, and one of few in the cerebral cortex, that are profusely spiny.
source: Second, they are the only class of interneuron in the PCx, and one of few in the cerebral cortex, that are profusely spiny (Haberly, 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Spines are important for synaptic plasticity.
source: Given the importance of spines for synaptic plasticity (Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1999; Maletic-Savatic et al., 1999; Toni et al., 1999; Matsuzaki et al., 2004; Tonnesen et al., 2014), HZ cells are poised to receive learning-dependent synaptic excitation, which in turn may allow them to exert adjustable inhibitory control over neurons in their neighborhood.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.
